tierWindow.goal: Understand what academic searching is and treat it as a planned discipline, so you can plan a simple search and identify keywords for it rather than typing a question into the first search box you meet.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Recognition, recall, description and guided application (understand and identify).
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Well-defined, one idea at a time; settled distinctions such as everyday versus academic searching, and the stages of a planned search.
tierWindow.autonomy: High scaffolding; worked examples; feedback confirms and explains; frequent low-stakes checks.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: No prior experience of searching as an academic discipline is assumed. The learner searches every day with Google and expects to type a question and get an answer; they have not yet met searching as something you plan, with keywords you choose on purpose. Teach from first principles.

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, what academic searching is: how it differs from the searching you already do every day. Second, the principles of effective searching: the stages a good search moves through. Third, planning and keywords: the first practical moves of a search you plan yourself. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This short course is about finding and using sources at university: what searching really means, and how to do it well. By the end you will be able to explain what academic searching is and how it differs from everyday searching, describe what makes a search effective, and plan a simple search by choosing keywords for it.

This is not a skill you can skip. Almost every assignment asks you to find and use sources, and the quality of what you find shapes the quality of what you write. Searching well saves you time and leads you to better material than the first result you happen to land on.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: explain what academic searching is, describe the principles of an effective search, plan a simple search and identify keywords.

practiceConnection.academic: Finding and using sources is the groundwork of academic study. Every essay built on reading, every literature review, every project that rests on evidence begins with a search. Build the habit now and it carries into every module of your degree, and into the research and fact-finding that professional work later asks of you.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced finding and using sources courses take you into using a library discovery service with Boolean searches, evaluating sources, and extending a search through databases and citation searching. Going wider: the same habits underpin Academic Writing, Criticality and Researching, where you put your sources to work on real tasks.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Finding sources is no longer hit and miss: it is something you can plan and do on purpose. You can explain what academic searching is, exploratory, iterative and strategy-driven, and how it differs from everyday searching. You can describe the stages an effective search moves through. And you can plan a simple search and choose keywords, with synonyms to broaden it. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, searching is something you do in every module. Each assignment that rests on reading, each project that needs evidence, begins with a planned search and well-chosen keywords. It is also a habit that professional life rewards: the ability to find, weigh and use good information travels well beyond your degree.

courseReferences.title: See pages 95 to 112 of Chapter 7, 'Research: Developing Effective Search Strategies', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
